welcome.script:
Welcome to Deckhand, a local presentation coordinator built for developers who present code.

The audience sees a polished OBS stream while you keep full control from your own screen.

Deckhand keeps four outputs in sync automatically: your slide deck, OBS scenes, the presenter stage, and the browser windows you need for live demos.

You drive everything from the keyboard or hotkeys, and the teleprompter tracks your voice in real time.

Let us walk through what that looks like in practice.

code-walkthrough.script:
Now we walk through the initialization flow in the terminal on the left.

The entry point is the run function at the top of index dot j s.

Notice how it loads the presentation config first, then composes the hub, the OBS client, and the browser session.

Pay particular attention to line forty two, where the coordinator is created with injected dependencies.

This dependency injection is what makes the whole system testable without a real Chrome process or a live OBS connection.

After the coordinator starts, it publishes sticky state that every presenter surface consumes.

Let us run the demo and watch the logs scroll by.

architecture.script:
The architecture follows a single source of truth principle.

One layout model drives OBS scenes, the presenter stage geometry, and the teleprompter simultaneously.

The hub sits in the middle as a local WebSocket server that drivers and observers connect to.

The coordinator owns the canonical runtime state and publishes it as sticky channels.

Hammerspoon positions windows on the presenter stage using exact CGWindowID bindings resolved at startup.

This means no fragile title matching or Accessibility polling in the steady state.

Every surface, from the console to the teleprompter to the freeze-frame transitions, reads from the same coordinator-owned state.

terminal-deep-dive.script:
Let us stay in the terminal for this section and look at the command flow.

The first thing to notice is how the coordinator enqueues slide operations to avoid overlapping transitions.

Each position change goes through a freeze, mutate, wait, reveal sequence that masks window resizing behind a still frame.

The reveal direction is computed from the previous and current slide indices, matching reveal deck ordering.

If the driver reports a settle event, the coordinator waits for it before revealing.

This ensures the deck has actually painted before the audience sees the new scene.

You can see the timing in the logs as each step completes.

live-demo.script:
Time for the live demo.

First, narrate the setup so the audience understands what we are about to do.

We start the application in the terminal and watch it boot up.

Then we switch the browser on the right to the home page so everyone can see the landing experience.

Notice how the browser navigation happens behind the freeze frame, so the audience never sees a flash of unstyled content.

The directional transition slides the whole frame into place once everything is settled.

This is what makes Deckhand presentations look polished even with live, unpredictable content.

api-demo.script:
In this slide we call the API from the terminal while the audience watches the browser respond.

The browser on the left has navigated to the API endpoint automatically as part of the slide transition.

We run a curl command in the terminal on the right and explain each part of the request.

The response comes back as JSON, and the browser renders it in a readable format.

This split layout is perfect for showing cause and effect between the terminal and the browser side by side.

The audience sees the result without you having to alt-tab or switch spaces.

It is one of the most effective layouts for live coding presentations.

browser-fullscreen.script:
Here we go full screen with the browser to showcase the final product page.

This layout gives the audience the maximum visual real estate for your web application.

The browser navigated to the showcase URL automatically when this slide loaded.

Take a moment to scroll through the page and highlight the key features.

The teleprompter on your screen keeps your place in the script, but the audience only sees the browser.

When you are ready, we will switch to the dual browser layout for a comparison view.

This is where Deckhand really shines, because every transition is smooth and directional.

dual-demo.script:
Now we have two browsers side by side for a comparison.

The browser on the left shows the checkout flow, while the one on the right shows the main dashboard.

Both tabs were activated automatically when this slide transitioned.

Walk the audience through the differences between the two views.

Notice how the focus indicator tells you which window Deckhand considers the primary one for this slide.

The freeze frame transition kept both windows hidden while they loaded their new content.

This dual layout is ideal for before-and-after comparisons or A-B testing demos.

That concludes the Deckhand walkthrough, thank you for watching.
